source.note: Generated by `--plan brief.md` with z-ai/glm-5.3-flash (second attempt; the first wrote done_threshold 1, out of bounds), then approved with these edits, applied by plans/approve_ja.py. (1) Every rubric came back best-first; the program reads level 0 as the worst, so each question's rubric and the fit rubric were reversed. The fit rubric was also reordered so that 'cannot be assessed' sits above 'irreconcilable conflict'. (2) per_dimension 1 -> 2, min_q 5 -> 8, max_q 8 -> 12, reserve_early 1 (unchanged): as written, coverage was met by the fourth answer and the budget ran to eight, so the judge chose almost nothing and `done` could not vary. Now 4 dimensions owe 8 answers, the budget is 12, and the pool is 16. (3) done_threshold 0.95 -> 0.5: the model's two attempts wrote 1 and then the bound's maximum, neither a considered number; 0.5 is the same provisional value the earlier 50-interview plan ran under. (4) Six questions added by the approver, written in the same style, so the pool exceeds the budget and some questions go unasked: two per technical dimension. A second generated draft failed validation twice and was not used. (5) ui text -> textarea, with text also allowed: these questions want prose. (6) One typo fixed in rust_readiness (聞かせます -> 聞かせてください). (7) done.true: 'at least once' -> 'at least twice', to match per_dimension. Nothing else was changed; dimension names and weights are the model's. The English plan is a translation of the approved Japanese plan made at approval time; ids, order, policy and rubric levels are identical.

answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: I work on the invoice processing module of our ERP suite, about two years now. We did run into a transaction boundary issue — invoice approval and the downstream ledger posting were happening in one big transaction, and it was locking rows other approvers needed. Our tech lead redesigned it so approval and posting happen in separate transactions with a status field connecting them. I implemented part of the new approval endpoint following his design, and I wrote the migration for the new status column, but the actual decision about where to split it and why was his call, not mine. I understood the reasoning once he explained it, but I couldn't have designed that split myself at the time.
answers.says: Has no experience making transaction boundary design decisions themselves. The answer stops at ‘the team decided’ or ‘a senior engineer designed it,’ and even when asked what part they were responsible for or what they considered, they cannot explain concretely. They claim Java experience, but the answer shows the design decisions were left to others.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: Our module had a slow query problem during month-end close, when a lot of customers run large batch approvals at once. The senior backend engineer profiled it and found a missing index on the invoice-status lookup table. I helped by pulling the query logs he asked for and confirming the fix worked in staging, but he's the one who identified the missing index and decided on the fix. I haven't led that kind of investigation myself yet — I've mostly been the person executing a diagnosis someone else already made.
answers.says: Explains that JVM and Kubernetes operations were handled by other team members or SRE, so they only wrote code and were never directly involved in operational problems. Even when asked about their involvement in triage or measurement, they cannot describe concretely what logs they looked at or what action they took.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: At my company, invoice payments go through our payment processor's API, and we use idempotency keys so a retry after a timeout doesn't create a duplicate payment record — the key is based on the invoice ID and a payment attempt number, and the database rejects a duplicate insert on that key. If a payment fails partway through, the standard approach is to mark it failed and let the retry logic pick it up rather than assuming success, and any correction after the fact is supposed to be a new adjusting entry rather than editing the original record. That's the general pattern as I understand it from working on the module, though I haven't personally been the one to design that idempotency logic or handle an actual case where it broke.
answers.says: Has no real example of duplication or a mismatch they personally handled; the answer stops at ‘the team handled it,’ and even when asked about their own role, they cannot explain concretely. Or, they cannot describe any experience handling a consistency mismatch at all.

answers.text: Tell me about an incident that occurred in a system you operated. Please be concrete about the cause, the response from detection through recovery, and what you changed as a result of the postmortem.
answers.answer: I haven't operated through an incident on a system I was responsible for myself. There was an invoice-duplication issue on our module before I joined that people still mention in onboarding, and I've read through the postmortem doc for it, but I wasn't involved in the actual response, so I'd rather not describe it as if it were my own experience.
answers.says: Has no experience with an incident in a system they themselves operated; the answer stays at what they heard or saw about an incident someone else handled. Cannot describe their own role concretely even when asked.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you restored data consistency in a production Java service after an incident or a bug. What was broken, how did you pin down the scope, how did you fix it, and how did you confirm the fix worked?
answers.answer: I haven't led a data-recovery effort myself. When we found a set of invoices with an incorrect status after a bad deploy, our senior engineer wrote the script that corrected them with new entries rather than editing the bad rows directly. I helped verify the list of affected invoice IDs against our audit log, but he owned the actual fix and the verification approach.
answers.says: Explains that restoring consistency was handled by a DBA or a different team, so they weren't involved. Even when asked about scoping or verification, they cannot describe concretely what they looked at or what they did.

answers.text: I'd like to check something from your earlier answers where you used the phrase 'as a team.' Within that, which parts did you personally decide and do yourself? Please answer the same question again, using a different piece of experience.
answers.answer: In the transaction-boundary change I described, my own part was implementing the new approval endpoint from the design and writing the status-column migration — the actual decision to split the transaction that way was my tech lead's. In the validation disagreement I mentioned, my part was surfacing the edge cases from support tickets and implementing the final agreed logic; the compromise itself came out of a discussion between me and my teammate, not something I decided alone. I don't have a piece of work yet where I made the core design call by myself from the start.
answers.says: Tries to describe their own role, but the separation is vague, no more than 'I was mainly in charge of implementation.' Cannot describe the boundary between the decision-making part and the execution part, and the same degree of vagueness continues in a different piece of experience. Technical names are accurate, but no real example of the candidate's own judgment ever surfaces.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I haven't used Rust at all, and honestly it hasn't come up much in ERP backend work, which is almost entirely Java. I know the basic pitch — ownership instead of garbage collection, meant to prevent certain memory bugs — but I don't have a concrete plan for learning it since it hasn't been relevant to what I do day to day. If a role needed it, I'd expect to start with the basics the way I did with Java early on, but I can't give you a realistic timeline because I haven't actually sat down and mapped it out.
answers.says: Has barely touched Rust and has no realistic outlook for learning it. Says they're ‘willing to learn,’ but cannot give a concrete plan for where to start or how long it would take to become production-ready. Cannot speak to boundary design for migration either.

answers.text: We don't do full rewrites. What kind of part do you think should not be moved to Rust? If you've ever held back the urge to rewrite something and kept it in Java or an existing language, tell me about that too.
answers.answer: I don't have Rust experience to draw the line from, but in general I'd guess you wouldn't move something that's still actively changing, or where the team doesn't have the skills to maintain it yet. I did hold back on proposing a bigger architectural change once — I wanted to suggest restructuring our approval workflow, but I realized I didn't yet understand all the edge cases well enough to know if it was actually a good idea, so I held off and kept learning the existing system instead of pushing for a change I wasn't sure about.
answers.says: Can correctly explain the decision criteria (change frequency, latency requirements, the team's familiarity, how easily a boundary can be cut, how migration is verified), but has no real example of making that call themselves, and the answer stays textbook.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a team's technical decision. How did you voice the disagreement, how was it decided, and what did you do after the decision was made?
answers.answer: I disagreed with a teammate's proposed change to how we validate invoice line items, because I thought it would reject some legitimate edge cases we'd seen in support tickets. I pulled up three real tickets showing the pattern and brought them to our review, and we adjusted the validation logic together based on that. I implemented the agreed version afterward rather than my original proposal, since the team's compromise handled the edge cases I'd raised while still fixing the original problem he was trying to solve.
answers.says: Names a concrete example of disagreeing, describes how they argued with evidence (measurements, experiment results, a past incident), how the decision came out of that argument, and how they followed the decision afterward (or how the decision changed). Can also describe not overturning it alone after the fact, or, if they nearly did, how they stopped themselves. If they've ever argued for a full rewrite out of technical preference, they can describe how they held that impulse in check.

answers.text: Tell me about a concrete incident where the numbers didn't match in settlement or reconciliation. What was off, by how much, how did you notice, what was the cause, and how did you correct it? Please also cover how you handled data after it was finalized.
answers.answer: I understand the general causes of a reconciliation mismatch — time-zone boundaries around when a batch closes, rounding differences between systems, a refund that arrives after a period was already closed — and that the standard fix is a correcting entry rather than editing the finalized record. But I haven't personally investigated a real mismatch and traced it to its cause myself; that's happened on our module, but it's been handled by more senior engineers before it reached me.
answers.says: Describes that a mismatch occurred, but someone else did the investigation, and they cannot explain their own role concretely even when asked. The cause and the fix end at 'it was handled.'

answers.text: Tell me about a time you improved latency or throughput in a production Java service based on measurement. Give me the before-and-after numbers, and if you tried something that didn't work, tell me that too.
answers.answer: I don't have a measurement-driven improvement of my own to point to. The query fix I mentioned earlier, from the missing index, made month-end approvals noticeably faster, but that was entirely the senior engineer's diagnosis and fix — my part was confirming it worked in staging, not identifying the problem or designing the change.
answers.says: The improvement was done by the team or other members; they were not directly involved in either the measurement or the change. Cannot describe concretely what they looked at to make the call, even when asked.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: I found a bug in a PR of mine the day after it merged — a validation check that didn't handle a specific invoice currency correctly — and I flagged it myself in our team channel as soon as I noticed, rather than waiting to see if a customer would hit it first. I've shadowed our on-call rotation for about five months and I'm about to start taking primary shifts. I've also spent time helping a newer intern understand how our approval workflow state machine works, which took a few pairing sessions but I don't think of that as separate from my actual job.
answers.says: Can describe a concrete example of sharing their own mistake or delay before it got worse — what, when, to whom, how it was communicated, and what happened as a result. Also names a real example of taking on on-call rotation, inquiry handling, or mentoring juniors as their own job (duration, frequency, approach), and can describe never having thought of it as ‘not my real job.’ Both are told as their own actions, including experience of sharing within a blameless culture.

fit.says: Considering what it would be like for this person to work here, they can be judged as someone who would act in line with all of our working principles (argue with evidence, then follow the decision; do not hide; money is not a test environment; operations and support are equal work; decide the boundary before you rewrite). Throughout the candidate's account of their experience, they consistently show a stance of sharing incidents and mistakes without hiding them, treating on-call, support, and mentoring juniors as their own job, never skipping review and deployment procedures even in an emergency, and carrying out migrations based on measurement and agreement while respecting the team's decisions.
